There is a very big difference between people whose wealth puts them at the cut off to be in the top 1.0% and those at 0.1%, 0.01%, et cetera. So, they will vary a lot.

Some are very successful entrepreneurs/businessmen like Bill Gates, Warren Buffett, Sam Walton, Ted Turner, etc. (Note that most of these didn't come from poor backgrounds, but they did personally establish their own vast wealth.)

Some are the beneficiaries of inherited wealth that has been competently managed. While there are a lot of these people, this category can be overstated. It is very easy to squander vast fortunes if you are not the sort of person to establish one in the first place. There are very few families like this beyond a handful of generations. And at any given point in time, the richest of the rich tend to be relative newcomers to the club.

There are also less successful, but still very successful people who accrue their wealth over time after doing well at a profession such as law, accounting, banking, etc. or through the ownership of smaller businesses.

Last, there are people who are simply very disciplined and wise about their money, who have normal middle class existences but save and invest until they have investment placing them in the 1%.

Those last two categories are no doubt the majority of the 1% by number of people, but the first couple categories no doubt have the majority of the 1%'s wealth.

There are two groups of 1%:

  • The top 1% of income earners. We know relatively more about this group because the IRS collects a huge amount of info annually about everyone's income.
  • The top 1% of wealth holders. We know relatively less about this group because outside of the tip top few hundredths of a percent (who are famous or in an index like the Forbes 400) most wealth information comes from surveys.

One of the biggest studies of the wealthiest Americans was from Prof. Thomas Stanley, Ph. D. who wrote of his findings in the popular book the Millionaire next door. His findings were that many tended to be frugal owners of their own businesses. Given the tax benefits of owning a business, that seems likely.

The top 1% of wealth holders. We know relatively less about this group because outside of the tip top few hundredths of a percent (who are famous or in an index like the Forbes 400) most wealth information comes from surveys.

Also because "wealth" is an ambiguous term who's meaning can be massaged to ajust the curve pretty much any direction you like.
